articles.title: Campus Library Hours Extended
articles.content:
The university library will extend its opening hours during the final examination period. From Monday to Thursday, the main reading room will remain open until midnight, and group-study rooms may be reserved until eleven. Library officials say the change responds to repeated student requests and a survey showing that evening is the most popular study period.

Students must still present a valid campus card after nine in the evening. The café on the ground floor will close at eight, and no new borrowing will be accepted after ten, although returns may be made at any time using the outdoor chute. Staff note that quiet floors will keep stricter rules: phone calls and group discussion remain limited to designated zones.

Not everyone welcomes the extension. Some student workers worry about late shifts, and a few faculty members argue that longer hours encourage unhealthy cramming. The administration has promised a review after the pilot term, including data on usage and safety. For now, most students seem relieved. As one sophomore put it, 'When the dorm is noisy, the library is the only place where I can think.'

questions.question: Why is the library extending its hours?
options: Because students requested it and evenings are peak study times
questions.explanation: 原文：responds to repeated student requests and a survey showing that evening is the most popular study period.

questions.explanation: 原文：Students must still present a valid campus card after nine in the evening.

questions.question: Which service ends earlier than the reading room?
questions.explanation: 原文：The café on the ground floor will close at eight.

questions.question: What is the administration's attitude toward the pilot?
options: It will make the extension permanent immediately
It will cancel the plan after exams
It will review usage and safety data later
questions.explanation: 原文：promised a review after the pilot term, including data on usage and safety.

articles.title: Second-Hand Textbooks on Campus
articles.content:
Every semester, piles of textbooks leave dormitories at a fraction of their original price. A student-run market now lists titles by course code, making it easier to match supply with demand. Sellers avoid shipping costs, and buyers often pay less than half the bookstore price.

Professors are divided. Some welcome the savings and even post required editions early so that second-hand copies circulate. Others warn that older editions may omit new problem sets or corrected errors. Publishers, facing declining new-copy sales, have expanded digital rentals and loose-leaf versions priced lower than hardcovers.

Environmental groups point out that reuse saves paper and transport emissions. Yet the system only works when courses keep stable syllabi. If a department changes a book every year, second-hand stock becomes worthless overnight. A modest solution is emerging: libraries keep a few high-demand titles on reserve, and departments announce multi-year adoption plans whenever possible.

questions.question: What is one advantage of the student-run market?
options: It matches titles by course code and cuts costs
questions.explanation: 原文：lists titles by course code... buyers often pay less than half.

questions.question: Why do some professors discourage second-hand books?
options: Older editions may miss new exercises or corrections
questions.explanation: 原文：older editions may omit new problem sets or corrected errors.

questions.question: How have publishers responded to falling new-copy sales?
options: By expanding digital rentals and cheaper formats
questions.explanation: 原文：expanded digital rentals and loose-leaf versions priced lower than hardcovers.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest to keep reuse working?
questions.explanation: 末段：departments announce multi-year adoption plans whenever possible.

articles.title: Volunteering Abroad: Benefits and Doubts
articles.content:
Short volunteer trips abroad attract thousands of students each year. Participants teach English, build facilities, or assist in clinics, often for two or three weeks. Supporters say the experience builds language skills, cultural awareness, and a sense of responsibility.

Researchers urge caution. Brief visits can create more disruption than help when volunteers lack training. Children may form attachments to visitors who leave quickly, and poorly planned construction sometimes damages local livelihoods. Effective programmes, studies suggest, are designed with community partners, last longer, and match tasks to volunteers' real skills.

Universities have begun to respond. Some now require preparation courses and post-trip reflection essays. Others prefer long-term partnerships with a small number of locations rather than many shallow projects. The goal is not to discourage service, but to replace the idea of 'saving' others with the harder work of listening first.

questions.question: What benefit of short volunteer trips is mentioned?
questions.explanation: 原文：builds language skills, cultural awareness, and a sense of responsibility.

questions.question: Why do researchers urge caution?
options: Because brief untrained visits can disrupt communities
questions.explanation: 原文：Brief visits can create more disruption than help when volunteers lack training.

questions.question: What do effective programmes look like?
questions.explanation: 原文：designed with community partners, last longer, and match tasks to volunteers' real skills.

questions.question: What is the author's main message?
questions.explanation: 末段：replace the idea of 'saving' others with the harder work of listening first.
